text: About 4,500 years ago, while Egypt was building its pyramids, a civilization was growing along
the Indus River in what is today Pakistan and northwest India.
We call it the Indus Valley Civilization, and it was huge.
It covered more land than Egypt and Mesopotamia put together.
It's biggest cities, Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro, were home to tens of thousands of people.
And these cities were... weirdly modern.
Streets ran in neat straight lines, houses were built from bricks of the same size, everywhere
for hundreds of years.
Many houses had their own bathroom, waste water flowed into covered drains under the street,
four and a half thousand years ago, underground drainage.
Some cities today are still working on this.
In the middle of Mohenjo-daro sat something archeologists call the Great Bath,
a brick pool, sealed with tar so it wouldn't leak. Nobody knows exactly what it was for.
Maybe ceremonies, maybe a very fancy swimming pool. What is this? A brick, sir. A nice brick.
It's bigger. One to two to four. Every brick. Every city. Every time. I was trying to be
creative. Hands it back. Be creative with pots. They even used standard weights for trading,
so nobody got cheated at the market. And they traded far. Indus seals have been found
all the way in Mesopotamia, in today's Iraq. But here's the mystery. These people wrote
on seals, on pots, on tags, hundreds of different signs, and nobody can read them. Not one word
to this day, squinting at a seal with a unicorn-like animal. Fish, jar, unicorn? Shrugs. Either
a king's name or a grocery list. So we don't know what they called themselves. We don't
kings, their gods, or their stories. Oddly, archaeologists haven't found grand
palaces or giant royal tombs either, just well-planned cities built for ordinary
people. Then, around 1900 BCE, the great cities slowly emptied.
